newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trigger for Iran sanctions now $20 million.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trigger for Iran sanctions now $20 million.

text.p: The United States must now punish companies that spend $20 million or more a year in developing Iran's oil or gas fields, a decrease from the $40 million trigger required by law last year, the State Department said on Wednesday.

The Iran Libya Sanctions Act, which came into effect in 1996, required the United States to penalise non-U.S. firms that invested $40 million or more in any year in Iranian or Libyan oil and gas, and called for the Iran sanctions threshold to drop to $20 million if Washington failed to spur its allies to slap sanctions on Iran in the law's first year.
Washington has yet to use the law, although deals involving Turkey, Canada's Bow Valley Energy, and French oil giant Total have tested the limits of the ban.
The U.S. State Department insisted that if there were any violations, it would tap the law. "ILSA is the law and we will apply it fully," said department spokeswoman Elaine McDevitt.
The threshold for sanctions on investments in Libya remains at $40 million a year.

By targeting non-U.S. companies, the law was meant to persuade Washington's allies to join the United States in isolating Iran and make the Tehran government give up its alleged support of terrorism and pursuit of nuclear weapons.

So far, European Union nations have only withdrawn their ambassadors from Tehran after a German court in April accused Iran's leaders of ordering the murder of Iranian dissidents in Berlin, which Tehran denied.

The law complicated U.S. efforts to promote the development of huge new energy supplies in the Caspian region -- a goal that President Bill Clinton highlighted last week during the visit of Azeri President Haydar Aliyev.
The scramble for countries in the Caspian basin, which the State Department estimates holds as much as 200 million barrels in reserves, has been to find viable export routes.
Iran came out a winner last month when the Clinton administration said it would not stand in the way of a Turkish deal to import natural gas from Turkmenistan on a pipeline through Iran.

"There's a lot at stake here, not just the transit fees to be earned," said Robert Ebel, energy and national security director at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. "There's a lot of leverage that comes along when you have a pipeline."

The Turkmenistan deal effectively replaced a more controversial $23 billion agreement that Turkey signed a year ago to import natural gas directly from Iran. "It was the best of two bad alternatives," said Kyle Simpson, a senior Energy Department adviser.
The U.S. decision left sanctions supporters wondering whether Washington was easing its isolation of Iran following the country's election of a relative moderate, Mohammed Khatemi, as president.
State Department officials have repeatedly said over the last two weeks there has been no change in policy toward Iran and that every case that tests the sanctions law will be reviewed separately.

Industry experts said decision on Turkey set a precedent that would limit the U.S. ability to discourage pipeline deals through Iran. "Suddenly it's all right for Iran to be a conduit," said Larry Goldstein, an oil industry analyst for Petroleum Industry Research Associates.
Washington has encouraged Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan to build pipes through Georgia to Turkey and the Mediterranean or through Russia to the Black Sea to avoid Iran.
An aide to Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, the New York Republican who has been an architect of the Iran sanctions, said lawmakers were considering ways to close the pipeline loophole.
"The goal has always been to keep hard currency out of Iran," he said. "We are not ruling out legislation."
